en.note:
The idea

A relative clause describes a noun: "the man who lives here", "the book that I'm reading". In English you choose between "who", "which" and "that" depending on whether it's a person or a thing. In Dutch the relative pronoun depends instead on the article of the noun, and the relative clause is a subordinate clause: the verb goes to the end.

de man die hier woont = the man who lives here.

Die or dat?

the noun is…pronounexample
singular de-worddiede film die ik zie
plural (always)diede boeken die ik lees
singular het-worddathet boek dat ik lees

What counts is the article, not whether it's a person or a thing: het meisje dat daar zit (meisje is a het-word, even though it's a person). In the plural it's die again: de meisjes die daar zitten. After iemand (someone) you use die.

With a preposition: people

When English has "with whom", "about whom", "to whom" (or "who ... with") and it's a person, Dutch uses preposition + wie:

de collega met wie ik werk = the colleague I work with.

With a preposition: things

For things you don't say met die or met dat: you make one word with waar + preposition. Careful: met becomes mee.

prepositionrelative formexample
met (with)waarmeede pen waarmee ik schrijf
over (about)waaroverhet verhaal waarover we praten
op (on)waaropde stoel waarop hij zit
in (in)waarinhet huis waarin ik woon

In speech the two parts are often split, a bit like English "the pen I write with": de pen waar ik mee schrijf. This is correct too.

Wat: after alles, iets, niets

After alles (everything), iets (something) and niets (nothing) you usually use wat: alles wat ik weet (everything I know), iets wat lekker is. After iets and niets you also find dat, but wat is the safest choice.

The verb at the end

As in all subordinate clauses, the conjugated verb goes to the end of the relative clause. If the relative clause sits in the middle of the sentence, the main verb comes right after it: De film die we vanavond zien, is interessant.

Watch out: typical mistakes for English speakers

  • Leaving out the relative pronoun, as English often does ("the book I'm reading"): het boek ik lees → het boek dat ik lees.
  • Using die for everything: het boek die ik lees → het boek dat ik lees.
  • Translating "who" with wie: de man wie ik ken → de man die ik ken. Wie only follows a preposition.
  • Translating "which" with wat: de fiets wat ik koop → de fiets die ik koop.
  • Leaving the verb in the middle: de man die woont hier → de man die hier woont.
  • Translating "with which" word for word for things: de pen met die ik schrijf → de pen waarmee ik schrijf.
en.vlaams: In spoken Flemish you often hear an extra dat after the relative pronoun: "de man die dat daar woont", "het café waar dat we zitten". It's typical of the spoken language; in writing use just die and waar.

g.die: that/which, but for de-words and plurals
